mcqs.question: A B+Tree has fanout 340. Why does that let it index 13 billion keys in only height 4, while a binary tree needs height ~34 for the same count?
options: Fanout of 340 means each node branches 340 ways instead of 2, so tree depth grows logarithmically in the fanout instead of in base 2 — far fewer levels for the same key count
B+Trees store keys in a compressed binary format that binary trees cannot use
Binary trees can only store integer keys, limiting their capacity
B+Trees skip storing some keys to save space, trading completeness for depth
mcqs.explanation: Height is logarithmic in the branching factor: log base 340 of 13 billion is about 4, versus log base 2 being about 34. Compression isn't the mechanism, binary trees aren't limited to integers, and B+Trees don't skip keys.

mcqs.question: What is the key structural difference that makes B+Tree, not B-Tree, the default for disk-backed relational databases?
options: B+Tree nodes never need to be read from disk at all
B+Tree internal nodes hold only routing keys (no row data), packing higher fanout per page, and leaves are linked for cheap sequential range scans
B-Tree cannot be balanced, while B+Tree always is
B+Tree only supports equality lookups, which is simpler to implement
mcqs.explanation: Keeping data out of internal nodes maximizes fanout per page, and the leaf linked list makes ordered range scans a simple walk instead of repeated tree descents. Both structures can be disk-backed and both are balanced by definition; B+Tree is actually better at range queries, not limited to equality.

mcqs.question: A `status` column has only 3 distinct values across 10 million rows, and each value matches roughly a third of the table. Why might the query planner ignore an index on this column entirely?
options: The planner never uses indexes on columns with fewer than 10 distinct values, by a hardcoded rule
Indexes cannot be built on columns with repeated values at all
Low selectivity means the index would still touch millions of scattered rows via random lookups, which costs more total I/O than one sequential full-table scan
The index is corrupted and needs to be rebuilt
mcqs.explanation: With ~30% of rows matching, index-then-heap-lookup for millions of rows costs more scattered I/O than a single sequential scan, so the cost-based planner correctly skips the index. There's no such hardcoded distinct-value rule, indexes can be built on any column, and this isn't a corruption symptom.

mcqs.question: You have a composite index on `(last_name, first_name)`. Which query can it serve efficiently via the left-prefix rule?
options: `WHERE first_name = 'Ana'` alone
Neither query can use this index
Only queries that filter on both columns with OR, not AND
`WHERE last_name = 'Kim' AND first_name = 'Ana'`
mcqs.explanation: Because the index is sorted first by last_name then first_name, a query anchored on last_name (alone or with first_name) can use the tree's order. Filtering on first_name alone gives no useful starting position in an index ordered by last_name first, so it can't use this index efficiently.

mcqs.question: Why does a B+Tree index lookup on a 100-million-row table often cost only about 1 real disk read in practice, even though the tree has height 3-4?
options: The root and near-root levels stay cached in the buffer pool because every lookup reuses them, leaving only the leaf page as a real disk fetch
The table has been sharded across multiple disks automatically
Modern disks can read all tree levels in a single physical operation
The database precomputes and caches every possible query result
mcqs.explanation: The small set of root and upper-level pages is shared by every single lookup, so it stays hot in the buffer pool; only the specific leaf page usually requires an actual disk read. This isn't about disk hardware tricks, automatic sharding, or precomputed results.

mcqs.question: A query filters a column matching about 40% of a table's rows, and an index exists on that column. What is the planner likely to do, and why?
options: Always use the index, since an index always beats a full scan
Use a full table scan, because sequential I/O across 40% of rows beats millions of random index-then-heap lookups at that selectivity
Use the index only during off-peak hours
Reject the query as unoptimizable
mcqs.explanation: At high match rates, cheap sequential scanning of most of the table wins over paying random I/O per matched row through the index. Indexes don't always win regardless of selectivity, there's no time-of-day logic, and the query isn't rejected — the planner just picks the cheaper physical plan.
